<dl class="radar-defs" aria-label="What each axis measures"><dt>Ensemble speed</dt><dd>How fast a batch of independent samples runs: uneven, regular, small and adaptive workloads.</dd><dt>Footprint and turnaround</dt><dd>What the work costs around the run: the memory it holds, the time to compile and the code to write.</dd><dt>Capabilities</dt><dd>What the libraries support beyond the ensemble loop: wide values, fused steps, control flow, small linear algebra, contractions, FFT, scatter and reductions, each against the libraries the feature card records.</dd><dt>Tensors and precision (qualitative)</dt><dd>Dense tensor maths, array-style code and half precision: where PyTorch and JAX lead.</dd><dt>One-sample authoring (qualitative)</dt><dd>Writing the code for one sample and getting derivatives of it.</dd><dt>Low-level control (qualitative)</dt><dd>How much of the execution you control from the tool&#x27;s own language.</dd><dt>Reach (qualitative)</dt><dd>Where the tool fits in: your arrays, deployment outside Python and extension to new targets.</dd></dl>

<p class="axis-note radar-note radar-note-lead">Every measured axis is the per-sample ensemble workload raptor is built for; dense tensor maths, training and half precision are the qualitative axes, where PyTorch and JAX lead. Outer is better; overlaps are complementary, not a ranking.</p>
<p class="axis-note radar-note radar-caption-control">NVIDIA Warp gives you near-total control of every kernel, short of raw CUDA. raptor hands that control to the engine on purpose, so compaction and the launch shape are decided at run time; the two are different trade-offs, not a ranking.</p>
<details class="radar-data radar-howto"><summary>How to read this radar</summary><p class="axis-note radar-note">Each of the seven majors is the plain mean of its minor axes (the detailed radar draws every minor), with equal weights and the same rule for every tool; a minor a tool has no reading on is left out of its mean and the major's marker is drawn hollow. Hover or tap a major to see its minors.</p><ul class="radar-howto-list radar-howto-majors"><li><strong>Ensemble speed</strong>: Uneven ensembles, Regular ensembles, Small jobs and Adaptive ODEs; measured.</li><li><strong>Footprint and turnaround</strong>: Memory, Compile time and Code size; measured.</li><li><strong>Capabilities</strong>: Wide values, Fused steps, Control flow, Small linear algebra, per lane, Small linear algebra, per team, Contractions, FFT, Scatter and Reductions; measured.</li><li><strong>Tensors and precision</strong>: Tensor workloads, Array-style programming and Half precision and below; qualitative.</li><li><strong>One-sample authoring</strong>: Single-thread abstraction and Differentiable kernels; qualitative.</li><li><strong>Low-level control</strong>: A single axis, so nothing is averaged; qualitative.</li><li><strong>Reach</strong>: Works with your arrays, Deploy outside Python and Extensibility; qualitative.</li></ul><p class="axis-note radar-note">Each measured axis is stretched over its own best-to-worst range, so ring labels differ per axis (code size: at least 4x). Axes are grouped by theme, so read the axes, not the area.</p><p class="axis-note radar-note">Italic axes are the author's judgement, not measurements: hollow markers, a linear scale, and no marker where a tool has no reading. A hollow marker on a measured axis means a minor is missing. The hover panel has each axis's full wording.</p><p class="axis-note radar-note"><a href="https://amasat01.github.io/eagle/content/performance.html">Every number, in the full tables</a>.</p></details>
